title: The Wall at the End of the World
bullets: In 1400 the open ocean was a wall, not because anyone thought the Earth was flat — educated people knew it was a sphere — but because the winds that blew you out were assumed to be winds that would never let you back.

The civilization best placed to cross that wall, Ming China, had just decided not to: the eunuch admiral Zheng He led seven vast Indian Ocean fleets between 1405 and 1433, then the voyages stopped, the shipyards fell idle, and China turned its back on the sea.

Why Portugal and not a giant like France, England, or the Ottomans? A tiny, poor kingdom on Europe's southwestern corner, it faced only the Atlantic, was full of deep-water fishermen, and had absorbed Arab and Mediterranean navigation.
In 1385 the House of Aviz won the crown in battle as John I, founding a restless dynasty hungry for glory and income — and his sons found their project across the strait in Africa.

The age began with a raid: in 1415 Portugal stormed Ceuta, a Muslim port and the Mediterranean end of the trans-Saharan gold trade, capturing the faucet only to watch the caravans reroute and the water stop.

Ceuta still mattered, because it showed the Aviz princes where the gold came from — far to the south, beyond the desert — and seeded the idea that a ship sailing down Africa's Atlantic coast might reach the source directly.

Prince Henry the Navigator became the symbol of the enterprise, though the legend outran the man: he rarely went to sea after Ceuta, and the famous 'School of Sagres' is largely myth — he was a deep-pocketed sponsor, not a navigator.

Henry's real achievement was turning exploration from a one-off gamble into a sustained, repeatable state project, each voyage's hard-won knowledge of winds and currents fed into the next — the least glamorous part of the story and the most important.

title: Crawling Down Africa
bullets: The hardest thing about sailing into the unknown was not the unknown — it was getting back, since a favorable wind out meant a contrary wind home, the real wall at the edge of the world.
The caravel solved the machine half: small enough to nose into shallow coasts and cheap enough to lose, its borrowed lateen sail let a ship tack at an angle into the wind and claw its way home.
Cape Bojador was the nerve half — a low Saharan headland everyone 'knew' was where the sea boiled and monsters waited, though the real fear was the southward wind and current beyond it.
In 1434 Gil Eanes broke the spell by swinging wide of the shoals, finding ordinary ocean past the cape, and coming home alive — proving the terrible barrier was a bluff.

The single most important idea in the book was the volta do mar, the counterintuitive 'turn of the sea': to sail home you first sailed away from home, out into the open Atlantic, to catch the homeward westerlies.

The Portuguese learned the wind loop by getting flung around in it, settling Madeira (from around 1420) and the Azores (by the early 1430s) — the first overseas real estate and waypoints that made the ocean a neighborhood.

Madeira's sugar cane became the quiet prototype of the plantation: a single cash crop for distant markets, worked by an increasingly enslaved workforce — the shadow that would fall over the whole story.
The pace was the truest thing about it: decades to creep from Bojador to the Senegal River to Sierra Leone — the tortoise beating the hare because China's hare had gone home.

By the time the coast turned green and populous, two things had changed: the desert dread was gone, and in the 1440s the voyages finally turned a profit — paying partly in gold dust and partly in human beings.

title: Gold, God, and the First Slaves
bullets: This is where the Age of Exploration acquired its second face: once the African voyages began to pay in the 1440s, exploration and enslavement braided together so tightly that one cannot honestly be told without the other.

The Portuguese were after gold, not people — the gold that had crossed the Sahara by caravan for centuries from the rich states of West Africa, with the rising Songhai Empire then the dominant power of the interior.

The coast was neither empty nor primitive: in Senegambia the Portuguese met organized states like the Jolof Empire, with kings, courts, taxes, and a slave trade of their own — a world the Venetian Cadamosto described with admiring detail.

In 1444 a fleet returned to Lagos with some 235 enslaved Africans auctioned on the dock; the chronicler Zurara recorded both the families torn apart and the smooth claim that baptism saved their souls — the moral signature of the whole enterprise.

What was new was not slavery, which was ancient and universal, but its shape: a maritime, Atlantic, European-run trade by sea from the African coast that would grow over four centuries into a horror carrying more than twelve million people.

It grew because it was profitable and the profit had somewhere to go — the sugar plantations of Madeira and the Atlantic islands, where cash crop, consolidated land, and enslaved labor first locked together into a system.

Past Senegambia the Portuguese did what they did best: not conquer territory but seize and fortify the points where trade happened, raising Elmina Castle in 1482 — a strongbox for gold whose dungeons would later hold a far more terrible cargo.

In 1483 Diogo Cão reached the Kingdom of Kongo, beginning a relationship of embassies and baptism — Afonso I made it a Christian monarchy by choice — until the slave trade hollowed it out from the inside.

Down the coast marched the padrões — carved stone pillars, claim-marker and cross and granite press release in one — mileposts of the patient, inch-by-inch creep that reached Namibia before the great breakthrough.

title: Rounding the Cape
bullets: Underneath every voyage sat one terrifying question — where am I? — that got harder the farther the ships sailed out of sight of any coast.
The breakthrough was reading latitude from the sky: measuring the height of the Pole Star, then the noon sun, converted into a position using the printed star tables of the astronomer Regiomontanus.

The squinting was done with crude instruments — the heavy brass mariner's astrolabe, hung from the thumb, and the cheaper cross-staff, which slowly blinded the navigators who stared at the sun through it.

Longitude — east-west position — nobody could solve, because it needed an accurate shipboard clock that wouldn't exist until the 1700s, so navigators sailed by dead reckoning and stumbled onto things by accident.
John II, the 'Perfect Prince,' ran exploration like an intelligence operation — pouring money into the southern push and guarding Portuguese charts like military codes.

In 1487 he sent the Arabic-speaking agent Pêro da Covilhã, disguised as a Muslim merchant, overland to scout the Indian Ocean spice ports — mapping the destination by land while the ships fought toward the door by sea.

Tangled into the espionage was the medieval legend of Prester John, a lost Christian priest-king who could catch Islam in a pincer — a fantasy named in royal instructions, and one Covilhã was sent to find.
In 1488 Bartolomeu Dias was blown around the bottom of Africa by a storm without seeing the turn, reached the Indian Ocean, and was forced back by his frightened crew just short of India.
Dias named the point the Cape of Storms; King John, grasping that the sea road to the East was now open, renamed it the Cape of Good Hope — the wall had become a doorway.

title: Columbus and the Spanish Gamble
bullets: While Portugal worked patiently around Africa, a stubborn, self-taught Genoese mariner was peddling the opposite idea: sail west across the Atlantic and come around the back of the globe straight to Asia.
Europe's hunger for Asian spices had a supply problem sharpened by the Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453, which made a sea road bypassing the Muslim middlemen feel worth almost any gamble.

Columbus's pitch rested on a mistake, and the popular version gets it backwards: educated Europeans knew the Earth was round, but the experts were right that the ocean was vast and Columbus wrong that it was small.

He was rescued from his fatal error by a continent he didn't know was there, sitting at almost exactly the distance his wrong math predicted Asia would be — the single luckiest accident in the history of the world.

After years of rejection — including a flat no from Portugal's John II — his gamble landed before Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon, who said yes in 1492, the hinge year when the fall of Granada freed up crusading momentum.

He sailed in August 1492 with three ships and about ninety men, and before dawn on October 12 made landfall in the Bahamas, believing to his death he had reached Asia — and calling the people he met 'Indians' by permanent mistake.

The people he actually met were the Taíno: not a passive backdrop but a civilization of organized chiefdoms led by caciques, farming cassava and maize, who gave us the words canoe, hammock, barbecue, hurricane, and tobacco.

The first reckoning came at La Navidad, the fort built from the wrecked Santa María's timbers: the thirty-nine men left behind seized women and gold and were wiped out by the Taíno — welcome, abuse, and violent reckoning in miniature.

Columbus made four voyages, governed Hispaniola so brutally he was shipped home in chains, and died in 1506 still insisting he had reached Asia, never knowing he had opened contact between two long-separated halves of the planet.

title: A Line Drawn Around the World
bullets: In one of history's great pieces of effrontery, two small kingdoms divided the entire non-Christian world between just the two of them along a line drawn down a globe no one had finished mapping.

The carving began with the Church: under the theory of the day the pope could grant Christian monarchs non-Christian lands in exchange for conversion, and the Spanish Borgia pope Alexander VI obliged with the transparently pro-Spanish bulls of donation.

Furious, Portugal ignored the pope and renegotiated ruler to ruler, and the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas moved the line west — to a meridian 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands — splitting the unexplored world in two.
The line had teeth despite being unfindable: with longitude unsolved, the two crowns divided the world along a boundary they were physically incapable of locating at sea.

Its strangest gift was Brazil: in 1500 Cabral, swinging west to round Africa, bumped into the South American bulge, which happened to fall on Portugal's side of the line — the literal reason Brazil speaks Portuguese.
The Florentine Amerigo Vespucci did what Columbus never managed — looked at the immense southern coastline, changed his mind, and argued in print that this was a mundus novus, a whole new continent.

Vespucci's claim torn up the basic architecture of the map: for thousands of years Europeans had believed in three connected lands, and now there was a fourth, sitting in an ocean everyone had assumed was empty.

In 1507 the cartographer Martin Waldseemüller printed the new continent as separate from Asia and labeled it 'America' for Amerigo's first name — so the lands Columbus reached were named not for him but for the man who understood what they were.

In about fifteen years Europeans went from thinking the western ocean led to Asia, to carving up an imaginary world, to grasping it was a new quarter of the Earth — the conceptual turning point of the whole book.

title: Da Gama Forces the Indian Ocean
bullets: When the Portuguese sailed through Dias's door into the Indian Ocean, they discovered nothing: it was already the busiest, richest, most cosmopolitan trading world on the planet, and they were the crude, marginal newcomers muscling in.

Vasco da Gama, sent by King Manuel I in 1497, sailed up the East African coast and found not a primitive shore but the Swahili coast — wealthy, stone-built, Muslim trading cities like Mombasa, Malindi, and Kilwa, full participants in Indian Ocean trade.

The open ocean ran on the monsoon, and da Gama's famous 'discovery' was completed by an Indian Ocean pilot from Malindi using a thousand years of Asian and Arab knowledge — the route rode on the back of the East's own seafaring.

At Calicut in May 1498, the cosmopolitan Hindu Zamorin's officials reportedly laughed at da Gama's gifts — striped cloth, hats, coral beads — revealing the galling truth: Europe was poor and had nothing the East needed.
The voyage was a commercial triumph anyway — one cargo of pepper returned many times the cost of the whole expedition — proving a route so profitable it was worth holding by force.
Portugal's answer to having nothing to sell was to become a predator: using its one advantage, ships built to carry heavy cannon, to seize, tax, and monopolize the trade itself.
Viceroy Almeida proved the naval strategy at the Battle of Diu in 1509, smashing a combined Mamluk, Gujarati, and Venetian fleet and establishing Portuguese supremacy across the ocean's sea lanes.

Albuquerque built the empire of choke-points — Goa (1510), Malacca (1511), and Hormuz (1515) — holding the doors so a kingdom of a million could dominate a region of tens of millions without occupying it.
Portugal built a seaborne empire of forts and fleets, a planetary protection racket skimming an existing economy — the opposite of the territorial empire Spain was building in the Americas.

title: The Pacific and the First Circle
bullets: By the 1510s the European world map was a mess of half-truths, with one enormous question hanging over it: what lay between the New World and Asia?

The answer came in two stages — the first a glimpse from a mountaintop, in 1513, when Vasco Núñez de Balboa crossed the Isthmus of Panama, saw open water to the south, and claimed the entire ocean for Spain.

Balboa's discovery proved the New World was a barrier with another whole ocean behind it, and raised the prize question: was there a passage through or around the Americas to reach the Spice Islands from the west?
Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese nobleman who had fallen out with his own king, sailed in 1519 for Spain under Charles V with five ships and about 270 men to find that western passage.

After crushing a mutiny among captains who resented a Portuguese commander, Magellan found the freezing, maze-like strait at the bottom of South America that now bears his name, and named the calm sea beyond it the Pacific — the cruelest misnomer in geography.

Nobody had grasped the Pacific's vastness: for three months and twenty days the starving crews ate the leather off the rigging, sawdust, and rats, and died above all of scurvy, the great unsolved killer of the age.

At Mactan in the Philippines in 1521, the chieftain Lapulapu refused to submit and his warriors cut Magellan down in the surf — so the famous first man to circle the globe never actually completed the circle.
The survivors closed the loop under the Basque captain Juan Sebastián Elcano, whose Victoria limped into Seville in September 1522 with just eighteen gaunt men out of the roughly 270 who had sailed.

We know the voyage at all because the Italian Antonio Pigafetta kept a journal through the whole ordeal — proving, with their own bodies as the cost, that the Earth was a single connected globe that could be sailed all the way around.

title: The Fall of the Aztecs
bullets: The conquest of the Aztecs is the most famous and most misunderstood episode in the book: not a fairy tale of a few Spaniards toppling an empire by superior technology, but a civil war decided in the end by a microbe.

The empire belonged to the Mexica, whose capital Tenochtitlan was one of the largest cities on Earth — a lake metropolis of perhaps 200,000, with causeways, canals, floating gardens, and an aqueduct, that dwarfed any city in Spain.
The Mexica ran a tribute empire that forced subjugated peoples to send goods and sacrificial victims to Tenochtitlan — and the resentment of the conquered was the crack the Spanish would pry open.
Hernán Cortés landed in 1519 with about 500 men in open defiance of the Cuban governor, reportedly scuttled his own ships so there was no going back, and won by politics rather than technology.

His political genius depended on two things the supremacy myth erases: La Malinche, the enslaved Nahua interpreter without whom Cortés could not have spoken a word in Mexico, and the alliance with the Mexica-hating Tlaxcala.

Cortés's real army was indigenous — tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan and other native warriors with the Spaniards as a small armored core — so the conquest was, in large part, a rebellion of the empire's own oppressed subjects.

The first phase nearly worked and then collapsed: Cortés took the emperor Moctezuma hostage, but a massacre during his absence triggered the furious night of escape, the Noche Triste, in which the Mexica nearly annihilated the invaders.

What saved the conquest was smallpox, which arrived in 1520 and tore through a people with no resistance, killing perhaps a third of central Mexico in a year or two and gutting the Mexica's ability to fight while the immune Spanish walked through untouched.

Cortés returned and laid a methodical siege; Tenochtitlan fell in August 1521, the last emperor Cuauhtémoc was captured, and the Spanish built Mexico City and their cathedral literally on top of the ruins.
Much of what we know survives by a sharp irony — the Florentine Codex, compiled by a missionary bent on stamping out the very religion his Nahua scribes and artists recorded.

title: The Fall of the Inca
bullets: A decade after Tenochtitlan, the grim pattern repeated against an even bigger prize, brought down by an even smaller band of Spaniards exploiting an even more catastrophic stroke of luck.

The Inca Empire was the largest state ever built in the Americas — some 2,500 miles down the Andes, binding ten to twelve million people under a divine emperor — and it did it without writing, wheels, draft animals, or money.

What the Inca had instead was a genius for organization: tens of thousands of miles of paved roads, rope bridges, relay runners, famine storehouses, and a command economy fed by the mita, a rotating labor obligation the Spanish would later pervert.

By the time the Spanish arrived the head was already wounded: smallpox raced ahead of them, reached the Andes around 1527, and killed the emperor Huayna Capac and his heir before any Spaniard was seen.

Their deaths threw the empire into a brutal civil war between Atahualpa and his half-brother Huáscar, so that the conquest happened not despite the empire's strength but because disease and civil war had already gutted it.

Francisco Pizarro, an illiterate hardbitten old soldier, landed in 1532 with fewer than 200 men and marched up to Cajamarca, where Atahualpa waited with an army of thousands fresh from winning the civil war.

At Cajamarca in November 1532 the Spanish ambushed Atahualpa's largely unarmed retinue, slaughtered thousands in a few hours, and seized the god-emperor alive — decapitating the largest empire in the Americas in a single afternoon.
Atahualpa offered the largest ransom in history — a room filled once with gold and twice with silver — and the Spanish took it all and garrotted him anyway in 1533 after a sham trial.

The conquest was far from finished: Manco Inca rose in a great rebellion in 1536, nearly destroyed the Cusco garrison, then withdrew to found the defiant Neo-Inca state at Vilcabamba, which held out for a generation.

Not until 1572 did the Spanish storm Vilcabamba and behead the last emperor Túpac Amaru — the forty-year resistance correcting the lie that the native empires were hollow and the Europeans irresistible.

title: The Silver Engine
bullets: After all the motion of the previous chapters, this is what the motion was for, and the answer is a single word: silver — the thing that actually created the first global economy.

The mountain was found in 1545 at Potosí in the Andes — the Cerro Rico, possibly the most productive source of silver in human history — and around it, at over 13,000 feet, exploded a city of over 100,000, bigger than London or Seville.

The silver was dug by conscripted Andean bodies through the cruelest perversion in the book: the Spanish bent the old Inca mita into a forced rotating draft that marched men hundreds of miles to die in the mines and the mercury that processed the ore.

Spain built a formidable bureaucracy to move the treasure: the Casa de Contratación in Seville licensed every ship and cargo, the king took his royal fifth, and the armed treasure fleets convoyed the silver home against pirates.

In 1565 the engine closed a loop around the globe: the Manila galleon carried American silver west across the Pacific to trade for Chinese silk and porcelain, linking the Americas, Asia, and Europe in one continuous circuit.

China's insatiable hunger for silver — adopted as the basis of its money under the Single Whip Reform — meant the demand of Chinese taxpayers half a world away set the price that drove men into the mines at Potosí.

The instrument that tied it together was the piece of eight, the Spanish dollar: abundant, pure, and uniform, it became the first world money, spendable from Canton to London to Boston and ancestor of the dollar sign and the word 'dollar.'

The flood of silver produced the first worldwide inflation, the price revolution — and bitterly, Spain itself was among the worst hurt, the treasure flowing in one side and out the other to pay for wars while northwestern Europe quietly grew rich.

Many historians date the real beginning of globalization to around 1571, when the Manila route bridged the last gap and the world became, economically, one self-sustaining system bound by the daily flow of treasure.

title: Cross and Conscience
bullets: Every empire in the book sailed under a cross as well as a flag, and for many the religion was the entire point — the legal fiction handing out continents rested on the duty to convert the people who lived on them.

The spearhead of the new global Catholicism was the Society of Jesus, founded in 1540 by the ex-soldier Ignatius of Loyola — a disciplined, mobile, intellectually formidable corps that ran missions and schools from Mexico to China.

Francis Xavier carried the cross to the far end of the world, landing in Japan in 1549 to launch the first sustained Christian mission in East Asia — a journey unimaginable a single lifetime after Europeans feared a Moroccan headland.
Xavier opened Japan's 'Christian century,' until the authorities turned on the faith with violence — the first bloody sign being the crucifixion of the Twenty-Six Martyrs at Nagasaki in 1597.

Traveling with the catechism was a darker instrument: the Inquisition, which Portugal established at Goa in 1560 to police belief — its main targets not unconverted Hindus and Muslims but converts suspected of secretly keeping their old practices.

The conversion mandate that licensed the conquest cut both ways: if the natives had souls worth saving, they were human beings, and the very claim that justified the empire became the lever its critics used to condemn it.
The first cry came in 1511 on Hispaniola, when the Dominican friar Antonio de Montesinos thundered from the pulpit that the colonists were in mortal sin for enslaving and slaughtering the Taíno.

The fuse ran to Bartolomé de las Casas, who gave up his own encomienda and spent fifty years as the fiercest advocate for the indigenous peoples, pushing the crown to issue the protective New Laws in 1542.

The argument climaxed at the 1550 Valladolid debate — Las Casas arguing the natives were fully rational humans against Sepúlveda's Aristotelian 'natural slavery' — sometimes called the first formal European debate over the morality of empire.

It must not be oversold: Las Casas once suggested importing enslaved Africans to spare the Americans, a proposal he bitterly repented, showing the age's conscience had a hard limit that even fed the African slave trade.

title: The Northern Latecomers
bullets: For nearly a century the oceans belonged on paper to Spain and Portugal, until the English, French, and Dutch broke in — first as fishermen, then as pirates, and finally through a new invention that would own most of the future.

The earliest northern attempts chased a fantasy shortcut to Asia over the top of America: John Cabot reached Newfoundland in 1497 and found seas thick with cod; Verrazzano charted the seaboard in 1524; Cartier pushed up the St. Lawrence and named Canada.

A more aggressive strategy was simply stealing Iberian wealth, sharpened by the Reformation that split Europe into Catholic and Protestant camps and turned the rivalry between Protestant England and Catholic Spain into a near-holy war.

Francis Drake, half explorer and half pirate, sailed around the world between 1577 and 1580 as a plundering raid, falling on undefended Spanish silver ports and seizing loot that reportedly paid off the entire English crown debt.

The conflict came to a head in 1588 when Philip II's Spanish Armada of some 130 ships failed catastrophically against nimbler English ships and wild weather — shattering the aura of Spanish invincibility.
The first attempts to actually settle were near-comic disasters: the Roanoke colony simply vanished, leaving only the word CROATOAN carved on a post and an unsolved mystery.

What finally made the latecomers succeed was a better institution — the joint-stock company, which let many investors pool capital and spread risk, making enterprises too large for any one merchant possible.

Two companies changed the world: the English East India Company (1600) and the Dutch VOC (1602, the first publicly traded company) — corporations with the powers of governments that could raise armies, build forts, and wage war for profit.

These companies and crowns planted the colonies that lasted — Jamestown (1607), Quebec (1608), Plymouth (1620), New Amsterdam (1624) — anchored variously on tobacco, fur, and the search for a place to worship.

The latecomers were no gentler than the Iberians: in 1621 the VOC's Coen effectively exterminated the Bandanese to monopolize nutmeg, and by the time Tasman probed the southern seas and the Dutch settled the Cape in 1652, the Iberian monopoly was broken for good.

title: The World the Voyages Made
bullets: After two and a half centuries of voyages, the world was simply not the same world: the planet's separate biological and human spheres, cut off since the last Ice Age, had been welded into one.

The most sweeping consequence was the Columbian Exchange — the two-way transfer of plants, animals, and diseases that put horses and wheat and sugar into the Americas, and maize, the potato, tomatoes, chili peppers, and chocolate into the Old World.

The American crops touched off population booms — the potato feeding northern Europe, maize and the sweet potato fueling a surge in China — so a plant domesticated by Andean farmers helped determine how many people Eurasia could feed.

The exchange's second face was the deadliest event in recorded history: Old World diseases killed perhaps ninety percent of the indigenous population of the Americas, a die-off so vast some scientists argue the regrown forests measurably cooled the climate.

The emptying of the Americas drove the age's other great crime: the small Atlantic slave trade of 1444 metastasized into the triangular trade that forcibly carried more than twelve million Africans across the ocean.

Africa was no passive supplier: the Christian king Afonso I of Kongo documented the catastrophe in real time in elegant Portuguese letters and was ignored, and Queen Njinga out-fought and out-negotiated the Portuguese for decades in Angola.

Out of the collision grew new societies, and Spanish America met its blending with an obsessive racial classification — the casta system — injecting an architecture of racial hierarchy whose poisonous categories the modern world still carries.

The age changed how humans pictured the world: Mercator's 1569 projection let a navigator plot a straight course, and Ortelius's 1570 Theatrum Orbis Terrarum became the first true atlas, a planet held in one book.

It was one of history's supreme achievements and one of its supreme crimes at once — the same ships, winds, and ruthless little kingdoms did both — and we have been living ever since in the world they made.
